chapters.title: From a program to a system
topics: What does it mean to design a system?
HLD vs LLD vs software architecture.

illustrations.title: The application and storage work together
illustrations.caption: The application needs storage to keep a task after restart. We include both inside the boundary when discussing that requirement.
illustrations.why: Include the parts needed to explain the behaviour you are studying.

illustrations.title: Creating a task changes the stored state
illustrations.caption: Before creation, the collection is empty. After create(7, “Read”), it contains task 7, marked incomplete. The function returns the task details.
illustrations.why: Read the state before and after the operation to see exactly what changed.

illustrations.title: Save before reporting success
illustrations.caption: Memory-only tasks disappear after restart. In the revised version, the application commits the task before reporting success. The task remains after a process restart if committed storage is intact.
illustrations.why: Compare the two versions by restarting the process.

illustrations.title: Two levels of detail in one design
illustrations.caption: The high-level view shows the application and database. The low-level view shows the service, repository interface, and rules inside the application.
illustrations.why: Check that both views agree about saving a task before reporting success.

chapters.title: Organising code into modules
topics: Coupling, cohesion, modularity, separation of concerns.

illustrations.title: Shared storage details make changes spread
illustrations.caption: Several parts read or change the same task data directly. A change to a field or rule may therefore require edits in several places.
illustrations.why: Follow the arrows to find which parts know about the shared data.

illustrations.title: Separate responsibilities inside one process
illustrations.caption: The adapter reads input, the service checks task rules, and the repository saves and reads tasks. These parts all run inside one application process.
illustrations.why: Each kind of work has a clear place in the code.

illustrations.title: The service uses a repository contract
illustrations.caption: The service uses the repository interface. The SQLite adapter implements that interface. Startup code creates the adapter and passes it to the service; during execution, the service calls it.
illustrations.why: The dashed arrows show code dependencies. These objects can run in the same process.

illustrations.title: Each layer works at a different level of detail
illustrations.caption: The user asks to remember a task. The application applies task rules and requests a storage write. Storage uses files and the underlying device to carry out the write.
illustrations.why: Follow one request through the layers to connect the user’s action to the work below it.

chapters.title: From requirements to design choices
topics: Why the simplest sufficient design is often preferable.

illustrations.title: Turn “safe” into a checkable requirement
illustrations.caption: Create a task successfully, restart the process, and check that the task remains. This requirement concerns a process restart with committed storage intact.
illustrations.why: A specific requirement tells us which test to run.

illustrations.title: Choose, record, and review a design
illustrations.caption: Write down the requirements, compare choices, and record the decision. Later, use measurements and changed requirements to decide whether the design still fits.
illustrations.why: Keep the reasons for a decision alongside the decision itself.

illustrations.title: Check requirements before scoring preferences
illustrations.caption: Memory-only storage loses tasks after restart, so we reject it for this application. We compare preference scores only for choices that meet the required behaviour.
illustrations.why: An easy-to-run choice is useful only if it meets the requirements.

illustrations.title: Availability and durability answer different questions
illustrations.caption: A service may reply to requests yet lose tasks after restart. Another may keep every committed task but stop accepting requests while it recovers.
illustrations.why: Check both whether requests succeed and whether saved data survives the stated failure.

chapters.title: Drawing the system at different levels
topics: Architecture diagrams: C4 model, context, container, component, deployment, sequence.

illustrations.title: C4: zoom from the system into its code
illustrations.caption: Each step shows more internal detail. The dashed arrows mean “zoom in.” In C4, a container is an application or data store; it need not be a Docker container.
illustrations.why: Select the level that helps your reader answer a particular question.

illustrations.title: The application and database share one machine
illustrations.caption: The browser sends requests to an application on one machine. The database file is on that same machine. If the machine fails, the application and access to the file are both affected.
illustrations.why: Show physical placement when asking what can fail together.

illustrations.title: The task is saved, but the reply is lost
illustrations.caption: Task 7 is committed before its reply is lost. The client cannot tell what happened. A fresh create request may add task 8 unless the application recognises it as a retry.
illustrations.why: Trace the events in order to see why the client can be unsure even when a task exists.

illustrations.title: Each design change answers a new need
illustrations.caption: Add storage when tasks must survive restart. Add a remote interface when people need shared access. Extra machines require further decisions about data, failures, and load.
illustrations.why: State the requirement that makes each change necessary.

units.title: End-to-End Design, Architecture Reviews, and Evolution
units.example: Twelve complete architectural designs with a common 22-point review protocol.

chapters.title: URL Shortener

illustrations.title: Data ownership and relationships
illustrations.caption: Store link(id,code UNIQUE,target,owner_id,created_at,expires_at,state,version) and operation(owner_id,key UNIQUE,fingerprint,result_id). Code uniqueness is global within the chosen namespace. If data is later sharded, route by code or use an allocation protocol so uniqueness is not merely local to unrelated shards. Keep revocation and expiry authoritative and versioned.
illustrations.why: Identify identities, authoritative relationships, derived records, and the invariant that must remain true.

illustrations.title: The high-level path and responsibility boundaries
illustrations.caption: Place an edge or reverse proxy before replaceable application instances. A shared cache serves permitted mapping representations; the authoritative replicated store owns writes and recovery. A queue or log receives analytics independently. The cache is optional for correctness and must have bounded fallback traffic. Storage placement and acknowledgment determine durability; multiple web instances do not protect the mapping history.
illustrations.why: Follow the stated ordering and identify which step owns the relevant outcome.

illustrations.title: Naive path, failure, improved path, review
illustrations.caption: A code collision must cause an atomic uniqueness failure and retry, not overwrite the prior target. A cache outage must not flood storage without admission control. A lost creation reply must replay the committed operation result. A stale cache may serve a revoked link unless its policy limits that exposure. Analytics failure should reduce analytics freshness rather than redirect availability.
illustrations.why: Read this failure history alongside the naive design and the protocol; the surrounding text names the ambiguity and correction.

illustrations.title: Evolution follows demonstrated requirements
illustrations.caption: At roughly 100 requests/s, use one application and one transactional store. At 1000, profile and index before distribution. At 10000, add justified cache and application capacity. At 100000, partition or expand the measured bottleneck, protect cold-origin capacity, and test degraded operation. These levels are teaching checkpoints, not benchmark-proven hardware thresholds.
illustrations.why: Follow the stated ordering and identify which step owns the relevant outcome.

chapters.title: Rate Limiter

illustrations.title: Data ownership and relationships
illustrations.caption: Store bucket(scope_key,policy_version,tokens,last_refill,expiry) under an atomic update boundary. Track cumulative quotas separately if required. Integer or fixed-point units can avoid unnecessary floating-point drift. Policy changes need a rule for existing tokens and capacities. A distributed clock value supplied by an untrusted client must not let that client refill its own bucket early.
illustrations.why: Identify identities, authoritative relationships, derived records, and the invariant that must remain true.

illustrations.title: The high-level path and responsibility boundaries
illustrations.caption: Put coarse admission near the edge and resource-specific protection near expensive operations. For strict shared buckets, route updates to one appropriate atomic owner or a reviewed distributed mechanism. For regional approximation, allocate bounded regional budgets and state the overshoot behavior. Keep a global emergency cap and protect the limiter's own capacity; an overloaded protection service can otherwise become the first failure point.
illustrations.why: Follow the stated ordering and identify which step owns the relevant outcome.

illustrations.title: Naive path, failure, improved path, review
illustrations.caption: Race: two requests both read one token and both pass. Fix with an atomic transition. Clock rollback must not create extra refill; expiry should not unexpectedly grant an unsafe fresh burst. Store outage triggers the documented local-budget, fail-closed, or bounded fail-open policy. Policy inconsistency and key spoofing can bypass intended limits even when the bucket arithmetic is correct.
illustrations.why: Read this failure history alongside the naive design and the protocol; the surrounding text names the ambiguity and correction.

illustrations.title: Evolution follows demonstrated requirements
illustrations.caption: Start with a correct local bucket and deterministic tests. Move to an atomic shared owner when multiple processes require a shared cap. Add key partitioning for measured limiter load. Introduce bounded regional allocation only when latency or partition behavior justifies its extra protocol. Preserve the original policy meaning through every move, or version it explicitly.
illustrations.why: Follow the stated ordering and identify which step owns the relevant outcome.

illustrations.title: The high-level path and responsibility boundaries
illustrations.caption: Use replaceable connection gateways, a conversation-routed durable message path, a delivery log or outbox, recipient-routing metadata, and history storage. Gateways hold ephemeral connection state while the store owns messages. A delivery route can be stale, so clients must recover by durable sequence. A broker outage can delay online delivery without losing committed messages if publication intent is recorded atomically.

illustrations.title: Naive path, failure, improved path, review
illustrations.caption: Lost send response can duplicate messages unless stable client identity is deduplicated. Gateway failure drops connections; history remains authoritative. A slow client must be disconnected or degraded before its buffer exhausts the gateway. A membership revocation can race with cached authorization, so enforce the chosen revocation policy for delivery and history. Reconnect storms need admission and staggered retry.

illustrations.title: Evolution follows demonstrated requirements

Partition conversation ownership when storage or sequence pressure justifies it. Finally add regional placement only with an explicit message-order, membership, and failover contract. At every step, preserve stable message identity so retries remain safe.
illustrations.why: Follow the stated ordering and identify which step owns the relevant outcome.

stage: Complete first edition: all 22 units and all 12 mandatory case studies produced
scope: A complete illustrated reference edition. Workload, latency, capacity and price examples are explicitly assumed models; code examples demonstrate bounded mechanisms rather than production infrastructure.

figures.title: The application and storage work together
figures.caption: The application needs storage to keep a task after restart. We include both inside the boundary when discussing that requirement.
figures.why: Include the parts needed to explain the behaviour you are studying.

figures.title: Creating a task changes the stored state
figures.caption: Before creation, the collection is empty. After create(7, “Read”), it contains task 7, marked incomplete. The function returns the task details.
figures.why: Read the state before and after the operation to see exactly what changed.

figures.title: Save before reporting success
figures.caption: Memory-only tasks disappear after restart. In the revised version, the application commits the task before reporting success. The task remains after a process restart if committed storage is intact.
figures.why: Compare the two versions by restarting the process.

figures.title: Two levels of detail in one design
figures.caption: The high-level view shows the application and database. The low-level view shows the service, repository interface, and rules inside the application.
figures.why: Check that both views agree about saving a task before reporting success.

figures.title: Shared storage details make changes spread
figures.caption: Several parts read or change the same task data directly. A change to a field or rule may therefore require edits in several places.
figures.why: Follow the arrows to find which parts know about the shared data.

figures.title: Separate responsibilities inside one process
figures.caption: The adapter reads input, the service checks task rules, and the repository saves and reads tasks. These parts all run inside one application process.
figures.why: Each kind of work has a clear place in the code.

figures.title: The service uses a repository contract
figures.caption: The service uses the repository interface. The SQLite adapter implements that interface. Startup code creates the adapter and passes it to the service; during execution, the service calls it.
figures.why: The dashed arrows show code dependencies. These objects can run in the same process.

figures.title: Each layer works at a different level of detail
figures.caption: The user asks to remember a task. The application applies task rules and requests a storage write. Storage uses files and the underlying device to carry out the write.
figures.why: Follow one request through the layers to connect the user’s action to the work below it.

figures.title: Turn “safe” into a checkable requirement
figures.caption: Create a task successfully, restart the process, and check that the task remains. This requirement concerns a process restart with committed storage intact.
figures.why: A specific requirement tells us which test to run.

figures.title: Choose, record, and review a design
figures.caption: Write down the requirements, compare choices, and record the decision. Later, use measurements and changed requirements to decide whether the design still fits.
figures.why: Keep the reasons for a decision alongside the decision itself.

figures.title: Check requirements before scoring preferences
figures.caption: Memory-only storage loses tasks after restart, so we reject it for this application. We compare preference scores only for choices that meet the required behaviour.
figures.why: An easy-to-run choice is useful only if it meets the requirements.

figures.title: Availability and durability answer different questions
figures.caption: A service may reply to requests yet lose tasks after restart. Another may keep every committed task but stop accepting requests while it recovers.
figures.why: Check both whether requests succeed and whether saved data survives the stated failure.

figures.title: C4: zoom from the system into its code
figures.caption: Each step shows more internal detail. The dashed arrows mean “zoom in.” In C4, a container is an application or data store; it need not be a Docker container.
figures.why: Select the level that helps your reader answer a particular question.

figures.title: The application and database share one machine
figures.caption: The browser sends requests to an application on one machine. The database file is on that same machine. If the machine fails, the application and access to the file are both affected.

figures.title: Data ownership and relationships
figures.caption: Store link(id,code UNIQUE,target,owner_id,created_at,expires_at,state,version) and operation(owner_id,key UNIQUE,fingerprint,result_id). Code uniqueness is global within the chosen namespace. If data is later sharded, route by code or use an allocation protocol so uniqueness is not merely local to unrelated shards. Keep revocation and expiry authoritative and versioned.
figures.why: Identify identities, authoritative relationships, derived records, and the invariant that must remain true.

figures.title: The high-level path and responsibility boundaries
figures.caption: Place an edge or reverse proxy before replaceable application instances. A shared cache serves permitted mapping representations; the authoritative replicated store owns writes and recovery. A queue or log receives analytics independently. The cache is optional for correctness and must have bounded fallback traffic. Storage placement and acknowledgment determine durability; multiple web instances do not protect the mapping history.
figures.why: Follow the stated ordering and identify which step owns the relevant outcome.

figures.title: Naive path, failure, improved path, review
figures.caption: A code collision must cause an atomic uniqueness failure and retry, not overwrite the prior target. A cache outage must not flood storage without admission control. A lost creation reply must replay the committed operation result. A stale cache may serve a revoked link unless its policy limits that exposure. Analytics failure should reduce analytics freshness rather than redirect availability.
figures.why: Read this failure history alongside the naive design and the protocol; the surrounding text names the ambiguity and correction.

figures.title: Evolution follows demonstrated requirements
figures.caption: At roughly 100 requests/s, use one application and one transactional store. At 1000, profile and index before distribution. At 10000, add justified cache and application capacity. At 100000, partition or expand the measured bottleneck, protect cold-origin capacity, and test degraded operation. These levels are teaching checkpoints, not benchmark-proven hardware thresholds.
figures.why: Follow the stated ordering and identify which step owns the relevant outcome.

figures.title: Data ownership and relationships
figures.caption: Store bucket(scope_key,policy_version,tokens,last_refill,expiry) under an atomic update boundary. Track cumulative quotas separately if required. Integer or fixed-point units can avoid unnecessary floating-point drift. Policy changes need a rule for existing tokens and capacities. A distributed clock value supplied by an untrusted client must not let that client refill its own bucket early.
figures.why: Identify identities, authoritative relationships, derived records, and the invariant that must remain true.

figures.title: The high-level path and responsibility boundaries
figures.caption: Put coarse admission near the edge and resource-specific protection near expensive operations. For strict shared buckets, route updates to one appropriate atomic owner or a reviewed distributed mechanism. For regional approximation, allocate bounded regional budgets and state the overshoot behavior. Keep a global emergency cap and protect the limiter's own capacity; an overloaded protection service can otherwise become the first failure point.
figures.why: Follow the stated ordering and identify which step owns the relevant outcome.

figures.title: Naive path, failure, improved path, review
figures.caption: Race: two requests both read one token and both pass. Fix with an atomic transition. Clock rollback must not create extra refill; expiry should not unexpectedly grant an unsafe fresh burst. Store outage triggers the documented local-budget, fail-closed, or bounded fail-open policy. Policy inconsistency and key spoofing can bypass intended limits even when the bucket arithmetic is correct.
figures.why: Read this failure history alongside the naive design and the protocol; the surrounding text names the ambiguity and correction.

figures.title: Evolution follows demonstrated requirements
figures.caption: Start with a correct local bucket and deterministic tests. Move to an atomic shared owner when multiple processes require a shared cap. Add key partitioning for measured limiter load. Introduce bounded regional allocation only when latency or partition behavior justifies its extra protocol. Preserve the original policy meaning through every move, or version it explicitly.
figures.why: Follow the stated ordering and identify which step owns the relevant outcome.

figures.title: Data ownership and relationships
figures.caption: Store conversation, membership, message(conversation_id,sequence,sender,client_message_id,body,version), and receipt(conversation_id,user_or_device,delivered_seq,read_seq). Enforce an appropriate unique client-message scope. Presence lives separately with heartbeat expiry. Conversation ordering needs one sequence authority or a reviewed conflict model; wall-clock timestamps alone do not establish a stable total order for concurrent sends.
figures.why: Identify identities, authoritative relationships, derived records, and the invariant that must remain true.

figures.title: The high-level path and responsibility boundaries
figures.caption: Use replaceable connection gateways, a conversation-routed durable message path, a delivery log or outbox, recipient-routing metadata, and history storage. Gateways hold ephemeral connection state while the store owns messages. A delivery route can be stale, so clients must recover by durable sequence. A broker outage can delay online delivery without losing committed messages if publication intent is recorded atomically.
figures.why: Follow the stated ordering and identify which step owns the relevant outcome.

figures.title: Naive path, failure, improved path, review
figures.caption: Lost send response can duplicate messages unless stable client identity is deduplicated. Gateway failure drops connections; history remains authoritative. A slow client must be disconnected or degraded before its buffer exhausts the gateway. A membership revocation can race with cached authorization, so enforce the chosen revocation policy for delivery and history. Reconnect storms need admission and staggered retry.

figures.title: Evolution follows demonstrated requirements
figures.caption: Begin with persistent history and reconnect correctness. Add connection replicas and explicit routing. Introduce durable fan-out for higher traffic or groups. Partition conversation ownership when storage or sequence pressure justifies it. Finally add regional placement only with an explicit message-order, membership, and failover contract. At every step, preserve stable message identity so retries remain safe.
figures.why: Follow the stated ordering and identify which step owns the relevant outcome.

figures.title: Data ownership and relationships
figures.caption: Store intent, recipient preference version, template version, delivery task per channel or recipient, attempt, and provider-event inbox. A later preference change needs a rule for already queued messages, particularly where cancellation or consent matters.

figures.title: The high-level path and responsibility boundaries
figures.caption: Use a durable ingress path, preference/template access, channel-specific queues or partitions, bounded workers, provider adapters, callback inboxes, and an outcome store. Separate critical and bulk capacity where necessary. A provider outage should saturate only its allowed resources. Queueing is not reliability by itself: delivery intent, worker attempts, acknowledgments, and reconciliation must agree about ownership.

figures.title: Naive path, failure, improved path, review
figures.caption: A process can crash after sending but before recording the provider result, producing an uncertain outcome and a possible duplicate on retry. Use provider idempotency or lookup where available; otherwise expose the residual duplicate risk under the channel contract. Poison templates require quarantine, provider outage needs backoff and expiry, and forged callbacks must not mark messages delivered. Reconcile old submitted or uncertain records.

figures.caption: Start with one sender behind an injected contract. Add durable intent and a worker when loss or latency matters. Finally add provider failover and escalation only after uncertain-outcome and duplicate policies are explicit and tested.

figures.title: The high-level path and responsibility boundaries

A hybrid keeps ordinary writes manageable while avoiding synchronous fan-out to every celebrity follower. Control-plane model deployment is distinct from the feed-serving data path.

figures.title: The high-level path and responsibility boundaries
figures.caption: Use object storage for sources and immutable segments, a durable processing state machine and task queue, isolated transcoding workers, metadata storage, and CDN delivery. figures.title: The high-level path and responsibility boundaries
figures.caption: Use a regional location stream and spatial serving projection, a durable trip and assignment store, matching workers, offer delivery, and trip event publication. Partition geography for query locality while providing a protocol for drivers crossing cell boundaries. A global control plane can distribute configuration, but a regional assignment must not depend on stale independent copies of driver availability.

figures.title: Naive path, failure, improved path, review
figures.caption: Late location updates can move a driver backward unless sequence or version checks reject them. Two requests can select one apparent driver; only one authoritative claim may win. A worker paused past offer expiry must not complete stale acceptance. Lost notifications require status recovery. A map-provider outage should use a justified degraded ranking or pause offers, not create duplicate assignments.

figures.title: Evolution follows demonstrated requirements
figures.caption: Start with a correct regional assignment transaction and basic proximity query. Add location streaming and indexed candidates when query cost grows. Expiry and confirmation both check reservation identity and current version; an old expiry task must not release a seat assigned by a later reservation.
figures.why: Identify identities, authoritative relationships, derived records, and the invariant that must remain true.

figures.title: The high-level path and responsibility boundaries
figures.caption: Use a waiting room or bounded admission before reservation work, an authoritative event/seat ownership store, durable reservation state, payment adapter, outbox or workflow engine, and ticket read model. Cache event descriptions and advisory maps separately from authoritative allocation. Partitioning by event can preserve local seat transactions but a hot event remains a concentrated workload needing admission and contention control.
figures.why: Follow the stated ordering and identify which step owns the relevant outcome.

figures.title: Naive path, failure, improved path, review
figures.caption: Two users reading available must not both win. A process can crash after reservation commit but before reply; idempotency must recover it. Payment can succeed after the hold expires, and stale expiry work can arrive after a renewal or new reservation. Version-checked transitions and reconciliation prevent these from corrupting ownership. Email delivery failure must not imply ticket issuance failed if the ticket already committed.
figures.why: Read this failure history alongside the naive design and the protocol; the surrounding text names the ambiguity and correction.

figures.title: Evolution follows demonstrated requirements
figures.caption: Start with a correct transaction and repeat-key behavior. Add durable expiry and payment reconciliation. Introduce admission and advisory caching for launches. Partition independent events after measurement, and consider more complex seat allocation only if one-event constraints justify it. figures.why: Follow the stated ordering and identify which step owns the relevant outcome.

A ledger correction is a new authorized accounting event rather than an untracked rewrite of history.
figures.why: Identify identities, authoritative relationships, derived records, and the invariant that must remain true.

figures.title: The high-level path and responsibility boundaries
figures.caption: Use an authenticated API, durable intent/operation store, bounded payment workers, provider adapters, verified callback inbox, ledger boundary, and reconciliation scheduler. figures.why: Follow the stated ordering and identify which step owns the relevant outcome.

figures.title: Naive path, failure, improved path, review
figures.caption: Critical histories include commit followed by lost reply, provider charge followed by process loss, duplicate or out-of-order callbacks, refund timeout, and ledger commit failure. figures.title: Evolution follows demonstrated requirements

Attempts are not interchangeable with runs, and an old attempt must not overwrite a newer attempt's final state.

figures.title: The high-level path and responsibility boundaries
figures.caption: Use durable schedule storage, coordinated scanners or partition owners, a dispatch log or queue, bounded worker pools, lease/attempt state, and reconciliation. Separate timing control from execution capacity. A control-plane outage can delay new dispatch while running jobs continue; worker loss should leave a recoverable run. figures.why: Follow the stated ordering and identify which step owns the relevant outcome.

figures.title: Naive path, failure, improved path, review

figures.title: Evolution follows demonstrated requirements

figures.title: Data ownership and relationships

figures.title: The high-level path and responsibility boundaries

figures.title: Naive path, failure, improved path, review
